chapter.title: The model only talks. The agent does things.

cards.body: ChatGPT and an AI agent can run on the exact same brain. Only one of them can act. Picture a brilliant new intern locked in a room with a letterbox: slide a question under the door and a sharp answer slides back out. **A chatbot is that intern behind the door.** An agent is the same intern with the door open, handed a task and allowed to walk around the office.
cards.simpler: ChatGPT and an AI agent can run on the very same brain. But only one of them can act. Imagine a clever new helper shut in a room with a letterbox. You push a question under the door, and a smart answer slides back out. **A chatbot is that helper behind the door.** An agent is the same helper with the door open, given a job and free to walk around the office.

cards.prompt: You text your friend's intern, Priya: 'What's the cheapest flight to Lisbon on Friday?' She replies with a price and an airline. You text: 'Book it.' She replies: 'Here is how you would book it.' What is Priya behaving like?

options.text: An agent: she found the cheapest flight for you
A chatbot: she answers, then stops at the edge of doing
Both: answering and booking are the same job

whyNot.a: That's the brain, not the agent: finding an answer is talking. An agent would have held the seat.
whyNot.c: That's mixing the brain with the hands: answering is words; booking changes the world. Only the second is acting.

cards.reteach: The test is not how clever the reply is. It is whether anything in the world changed. A chatbot's output is words for you to act on. An agent's output is a changed world: a seat held, a file moved.

cards.title: The brain only writes
cards.body:
A *language model* is the brain: a program that reads text and writes the next text. That is all it can do. It cannot click, open a tab, or send a message. Even the smartest one is a voice behind a door.

A *chatbot* wraps that brain in a chat window. You type, it writes back, it stops. You'd think the fancy answers mean it did something. It didn't. **Every chatbot reply is a suggestion for you to carry out.** The booking, the email, the file: still your hands.
cards.simpler: A language model is the brain. It reads words and writes the next words. That is all it does. It cannot click, open a page, or send a message. A chatbot puts that brain in a chat window. You type, it writes back, it stops. The clever answers make it look like it did something. It did not. **Every chatbot reply is a suggestion for you to carry out.** The booking, the email, the file: still your hands.

cards.title: Two Tuesdays, one brain
cards.body:
Tuesday one: Marco asks a chatbot, 'Find me a dentist near Shoreditch with a slot this week.' It writes 3 names and adds 'call to confirm.' Marco spends 20 minutes on hold listening to pan pipes.

Tuesday two: Marco gives an agent the same sentence. The same brain reads it, but now it can ask for a web search and a booking. It searches, reads the results, picks one, books Thursday 4pm, and reports back. **Same intelligence; the only change was whether its hands were allowed out of the room.**
cards.simpler: Tuesday one: Marco asks a chatbot, 'Find me a dentist near Shoreditch with a slot this week.' It writes three names and adds 'call to confirm.' Marco waits 20 minutes on hold. Tuesday two: Marco gives an agent the same sentence. Same brain, but now it can ask for a web search and a booking. It searches, reads the results, picks one, books Thursday 4pm, and reports back. **Same brain. The only change was letting its hands out of the room.**

cards.prompt: Which of these three is an agent at work?

options.text: You ask an assistant to draft a complaint email. It writes a sharp one, which you copy and send.
You ask an assistant to clear your inbox. It reads each mail, archives 40, replies to 2, flags 1, and tells you what it did.
You ask an assistant to clear your inbox. It writes a 12-step guide to inbox zero.

whyNot.a: That's a chatbot, not an agent: it wrote words and stopped. You did the sending.
whyNot.c: That's still the intern behind the door: a plan is words too. Nothing in the inbox moved.

cards.reteach: Look at the inbox, not the reply. If 40 mails are gone and 2 answers went out, something acted. If you are holding a guide or a draft, the intern talked and you are the one about to do the work.

cards.title: Open the door, and risk walks out too
cards.body:
An *agent* is the same brain plus two things: *tools*, which are actions it may request, and a loop that keeps going until the job is done. It writes 'search for dentists', software runs the search, the results come back, it writes the next step. Round and round until it says 'done'.

That open door is the whole point and the whole danger. A chatbot's worst mistake is a wrong sentence you can ignore. **An agent's worst mistake is a wrong action already taken**: the email sent, the file deleted. Useful and risky rise together.
cards.simpler: An agent is the same brain plus two things: tools, which are actions it may ask for, and a loop that keeps going until the job is done. It asks for a search, gets the results, writes the next step, and repeats. That open door is the point and the danger. A chatbot's worst mistake is a wrong sentence you can ignore. **An agent's worst mistake is a wrong action already taken**: the email sent, the file deleted.

cards.body: Dana pasted a client email into a chatbot and typed 'reply to this and send it.' The chatbot wrote a lovely reply and ended with 'Sent!' Nothing was sent. It had no hands, only the habit of agreeing. Spot it by asking one question: what tool actually did the sending? **If you can't name one, the only thing that happened is text.**
cards.simpler: Dana pasted a client email into a chatbot and typed 'reply to this and send it.' The chatbot wrote a lovely reply and ended with 'Sent!' Nothing was sent. It had no hands, only a habit of agreeing. You can spot this with one question: what tool actually did the sending? **If you can't name one, the only thing that happened is text.**

cards.prompt: A friend says: 'I used an AI agent last night. I asked what to cook and it gave me a recipe.' What would make that story actually about an agent?

options.text: If the recipe was better than a chef's
If it had also ordered the missing ingredients from a shop
If the AI was a newer, bigger model

whyNot.a: That's the quality of the brain, not whether it acted. A brilliant recipe is still words.
whyNot.c: That's the same brain in a bigger size. Chatbot and agent can share a brain; the difference is the hands.

cards.reteach: Agent is a job, not a brain size. The same model becomes an agent the moment it can request actions and keep going until the task is done. A recipe is advice. An order placed is an act.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
A chatbot and an agent can share the same brain; the chatbot writes words and stops, while the agent is given tools and keeps taking steps until the job is done. **That is why an agent is far more useful and far more dangerous** in the same breath.

Tomorrow: 'Book me a table' is one sentence. Watch it become eleven steps.
cards.simpler: A chatbot and an agent can share the same brain. The chatbot writes words and stops. The agent is given tools and keeps taking steps until the job is done. **That is why an agent is far more useful and far more dangerous** at the same time. Tomorrow: 'Book me a table' is one sentence. Watch it turn into eleven steps.

cards.body: Open any chatbot you already use and type: 'Send my mum a text saying I'll be late.' Watch what comes back. If it's instructions for you, you just met the intern behind the door.
cards.simpler: Open any chatbot you already use. Type: 'Send my mum a text saying I'll be late.' Watch what comes back. It can write the message. It cannot send it. **If it hands you instructions instead, you have just met the helper behind the door.**

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain, in 2 sentences, why asking a chatbot a question is not an agent and why having it book the flight would be.
